newsitem.title: USA: Analyst sees stable, possibly higher gold price.
newsitem.headline: Analyst sees stable, possibly higher gold price.

text.p: Gold market fundamentals point to stability or possibly a gradual price increase over the next four to five years, research analyst Rhona O'Connell said Tuesday.
But O'Connell, with stockbroker T. Hoare & Co in London, said it was not justifiable to call a long-term sustained bull market because the market was too elastic.
Speaking at Platt's Metals Week 1997 precious metals conference here, O'Connell said a supply-demand shortfall had been filled by borrowed metal over the last two years.

"The figures that we have done would suggest that before any central bank or hedging or speculative activity comes into the market we're looking at a fundamental shortfall of between 350 and 400 tons annually over the next three to four years. Then mine supply does start to catch up," she said.
She said physical demand was starting from a higher level than mine supply and scrap supply and it was strong enough to keep that gap open.

"So on that basis, if people are concerned about central bank sales, I don't think they need to be particularly because there is something like a 400 ton per annum shortfall, which if the central banks feel the need to fill the gap, they can do so and it won't have an adverse effect on price," she said.
"It doesn't feel like it today when we're knocking on $340 an ounce. The market's obviously under some pressure," O'Connell said.
But she said the fundamentals "point to stability, maybe a gradual increase in price over the course of the next four to five years."

"Because of the volatility of demand with respect to volatility of price ... it is always arguable that after a $20 or $25 move things will stabilize. It is not justifiable to call a long-term sustained bull market because the market is too elastic," she said.

"But as and when the shorts start to cover their positions that will take some of the pressure off the market. It will add to the support that the physical market is trying to give it. It won't take prices back toward $380 or $400 -- I can't see how that can happen at all. But I think you'll find that we'll end the year in a lot happier state than we are this morning," O'Connell said.
